findings.title: Team admin/owner check uses && so only users who pass both checks qualify
findings.body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. The variable name says either role should be enough, but the `&&` means a team admin who is not an owner fails the check. Such admins are rejected with FORBIDDEN unless they are the organizer or an attendee. Use `||`, or a single admin-or-owner query.

findings.title: Any attendee can add unlimited arbitrary guests and trigger emails sent in the organizer's name
findings.body: Authorization lets any booking attendee call this mutation. Nothing checks booking status (cancelled, past, rejected), and the input schema has no max length on `guests`. So any attendee can insert arbitrary attendee rows and make the system send emails to any addresses, with the organizer's name and reply-to. This is a spam/abuse vector. It also ignores seat limits on seated events. Restrict who can add guests, cap the list size, and validate booking state.

findings.title: Calendar update uses the caller's credentials, not the organizer's
findings.body: The EventManager is built from `ctx.user`'s credentials. When the caller is an attendee or a team admin rather than the organizer, `updateCalendarAttendees` runs with credentials that do not own the booking's calendar references. The external calendar event then is not updated, or the call throws. The booking user's credentials are already loaded (`booking.user.credentials`) and should be used instead.

findings.title: DB write happens before an unguarded calendar update; a failure leaves inconsistent state
findings.body: Attendees are written to the DB first. `updateCalendarAttendees` is then awaited without try/catch. If it throws, the client gets an error even though the guests were persisted. No emails are sent, and a retry fails with `emails_must_be_unique_valid` because the guests now exist. Wrap the external update and emails so a failure there cannot leave this half-done state, or roll back.

findings.title: Emails use the raw `guests` list instead of the filtered `uniqueGuests`
findings.body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` receives the original input. Any submitted email that was already an attendee, or was dropped by the blacklist filter, is still in the list. Existing attendees whose emails were resubmitted are treated as new and get a fresh 'scheduled' email instead of the 'guests added' notification. Pass `uniqueGuests`.

findings.title: Duplicate and blacklist checks are case-sensitive
findings.body: The blacklist entries are lowercased, but the incoming guest emails are not. An address like `Foo@x.com` therefore bypasses a blacklisted `foo@x.com`. The comparison against existing attendees is also exact-case, so an existing attendee can be added again with different casing. Normalize guest emails to lowercase before both comparisons.

findings.title: sendAddGuestsEmails ignores disabled standard emails and seated-event attendee privacy
findings.body: Unlike the other senders in this file, `sendAddGuestsEmails` takes no `eventTypeMetadata` and never checks `disableStandardEmails`. Hosts and attendees therefore get emails even when the event type disables them. It also sends every attendee the full calEvent, attendee list included, without honoring `seatsShowAttendees`. On seated events that leaks other attendees' emails.

findings.title: Error toast fallback is unreachable and can show 'undefined:'
findings.body: `message` is a template string, so it is always a non-empty string and the `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback never runs. When `err.data?.code` is undefined, for example on a network error, the toast reads 'undefined: ...'.
